sections.h2: What does the Texas homestead exemption do for a homeowner?
sections.html:
It removes part of your home's appraised value from the base that local taxing units tax, so the bill shrinks even though the market value does not change. Appraisal districts set value as of January 1, so your status on that date drives the year's bill. The Texas Comptroller lays out three layers: a mandatory school district exemption, optional local exemptions, and extra relief for older or disabled owners.

Texas has no state property tax. Counties, cities, school districts and special districts set their own rates, and the exemption applies unit by unit. Two owners on the same street can therefore see different savings if their taxing units made different choices.

sections.h2: How much is the general residence homestead exemption?
sections.html:
School districts must give a $140,000 residence homestead exemption under Tax Code Sec. 11.13(b). Other taxing units may add their own exemption of up to 20 percent of appraised value, but not less than $5,000, under Sec. 11.13(n).

  • School districts: $140,000, required by state law.
  • Any other taxing unit: a local option of up to 20 percent of appraised value, with a $5,000 floor.
  • Counties that levy farm-to-market or flood control taxes: $3,000 under Sec. 11.13(a).

Ask your appraisal district which units serving your address have adopted a local option, because the Comptroller describes it as a choice each unit makes.

sections.h2: Who qualifies as the owner of a homestead?
sections.html:
You qualify if you hold an ownership interest in the home and live in it as your principal residence. You cannot claim a second residence homestead, in Texas or anywhere else.

Buying mid-year does not cost you the whole year. A buyer who takes title after January 1 can get the exemption for the rest of that tax year right away, as long as the previous owner was not already receiving it. Heirs who are not named on a recorded deed must give the appraisal district an affidavit of ownership interest, the prior owner's death certificate, a recent utility bill and any court record citation.

sections.h2: What extra relief exists at age 65 or with a disability?
sections.html:
Owners who are 65 or older, or disabled, get an additional $60,000 school district exemption under Sec. 11.13(c). Local units may adopt their own version under Sec. 11.13(d), and that local amount cannot be less than $3,000.

A disabled owner must meet the Social Security disability-benefit definition. A surviving spouse aged 55 or older may keep the deceased spouse's over-65 exemption in certain cases.

The same group also gets a tax ceiling, often called a freeze. Under Sec. 11.26 a school district may not raise the total yearly tax on the homestead of an owner who is 65 or older or disabled; the ceiling generally starts from the school tax imposed in the year the owner first qualified. A surviving spouse aged 55 or older may continue it, and it can move proportionately to a new Texas homestead. New improvements other than ordinary repairs can raise it. Counties, cities and junior college districts may adopt a similar limit under Sec. 11.261.

sections.h2: How does the 10 percent appraisal cap work?
sections.html:
After you first qualify, your homestead's appraised value cannot rise by more than 10 percent a year, apart from new improvements. Sec. 23.23 sets the taxable appraised value at the lesser of market value or 10 percent above the prior year's appraised value plus the value of new improvements.

The cap takes effect on January 1 of the year after you first qualify for the exemption. The cap limits appraised value, not your tax rate, so a rate increase by a taxing unit can still raise the bill.

Disabled veterans get an exemption on any one property they own, scaled to their VA disability rating. The Comptroller prints these amounts under Sec. 11.22.

A veteran aged 65 or older with a rating of at least 10 percent, a veteran who is totally blind in one or both eyes, or one who lost use of a limb may receive $12,000. An unmarried surviving spouse and children under 18 may qualify too.

Veterans with a 100 percent rating, or 100 percent unemployability, receive a total exemption on the residence homestead under Sec. 11.131, and an unmarried surviving spouse can keep it under stated conditions. Sec. 11.132 covers a homestead donated by a charity, with the percentage matching the disability rating. Sec. 11.133 gives a total exemption to the surviving spouse of a service member killed in the line of duty.

sections.h2: When and where do you apply?
sections.html:
File with your county appraisal district, not with the school district or the Comptroller. The general residence homestead exemption must be applied for before May 1, and April 30 is the last day for some other exemptions and certain special-appraisal applications.

  • Homestead exemptions use Form 50-114.
  • The disabled veteran exemption under Sec. 11.22 uses Form 50-135.
  • A veteran applying under Sec. 11.22 has up to five years after the delinquency date to apply; the surviving spouse of a veteran with a donated homestead has two years.

Appraisal notices for single-family homesteads go out around April 1, and the protest deadline is generally May 15 or 30 days after the notice is delivered, whichever is later. If the value on your notice looks wrong, the exemption and the protest are separate steps.

sections.h2: How does the exemption matter when you sell?
sections.html:
The exemption ends with your ownership, but the tax lien for the year does not. A lien attaches on January 1 to secure that year's taxes, penalties and interest, so unpaid amounts follow the property and are normally settled at closing.

The owner on January 1 is the person liable for that year's bill and can be sued even after selling. Bills are mailed around October 1 and are generally delinquent if unpaid on February 1, when a six percent penalty and one percent interest are added. A buyer who closes after January 1 can usually claim the exemption for the rest of that year if the seller had not received it.

If you are selling a house with back taxes, an heir property without recorded title, or a home you no longer live in, ask the tax office for a current payoff figure and the appraisal district for your exemption status before you set a closing date.

faqs.q: Is the Texas homestead exemption automatic?
faqs.a: No. You apply to the appraisal district, generally before May 1, using Form 50-114. A buyer who takes title after January 1 can get the exemption for the rest of that year if the previous owner did not have it.

faqs.q: Can I get both the $140,000 and the $60,000 school exemptions?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are 65 or older or disabled. The Comptroller lists the $140,000 general school exemption under Sec. 11.13(b) and the additional $60,000 under Sec. 11.13(c) for those owners.

faqs.q: Does the 10 percent cap lower my tax rate?
faqs.a: No. It limits how fast your home's appraised value can rise. Rates are set separately by each taxing unit, and new improvements can be added on top of the capped value.

faqs.q: Can a surviving spouse keep the over-65 exemption?
faqs.a: Sometimes. A surviving spouse aged 55 or older may keep the deceased spouse's over-65 exemption in certain cases, and may continue the school tax ceiling. Ask your appraisal district to confirm your situation.

faqs.q: What if I inherited a house and am not on the deed?
faqs.a: Give the appraisal district an affidavit of ownership interest, the death certificate, a recent utility bill and any court record citation. Those are the documents the Comptroller lists for heirs not named on a recorded deed.
